source: Li and Coblenz (2026) A Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Software Engineering Practice
finding: Professional developers spent most debugging time updating their mental model, not fixing. The model is revised as evidence arrives.
numbers: 12 percent reproduce, 57 percent mental model update, 13 percent fix, 18 percent validate fix. 7 professionals plus 5 streamers, 17 tasks. 1.65 fix-validate cycles per task. In 9 of 17 tasks the person returned to model update after testing a first fix.
limits: Observation, small N, self-chosen codebases, constructivist grounded theory (interpretive). Not a controlled test; no outcome comparison.
agent_relevance: Budget most steps for evidence gathering and model update. A failed fix should send the agent back to S2, not to a new patch.

source: Li and Coblenz (2026) A Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Software Engineering Practice
finding: Tracing mode depends on familiarity. Forward tracing dominates in familiar code; backward tracing in unfamiliar, long tasks. Low-familiarity people used version history and structure instead of reading code.
numbers: Forward tracing dominant for P2, P5 (about 50 percent or more familiarity). Backward tracing primary for P1 (<5 percent familiarity), secondary for P3, P4 (<20 percent). Avg 5.5 techniques per task. Most common technique: line-by-line reading (16 of 17 tasks).
limits: Individual-case evidence from about 5 participants. Familiarity is self-reported.
agent_relevance: Let the agent switch between backward (from symptom) and forward (from entry point) tracing by how much of the repo it already knows. Use git history when code knowledge is low.

source: Li and Coblenz (2026) A Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Software Engineering Practice
finding: Streamers made more process transitions than participants. Number of techniques used did not predict time.
numbers: Median 9 vs 4 process transitions, p = 0.014 (Mann-Whitney U). Technique count vs time: Spearman rho 0.10, p = 0.68.
limits: Streamers narrate for an audience, which may inflate transitions. Non-significant correlation with small N has low power.
agent_relevance: More technique variety was not shown to help. Do not reward the agent for using many tools.

source: Li and Coblenz (2026) A Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Software Engineering Practice
finding: The paper contrasts its finding with expert advice and with information foraging theory. Textbook advice to read everything first is not what professionals do in large codebases.
numbers: Cites Agans (read manuals in depth) vs observed avoidance of reading; Spinellis lists 66 techniques. Cites a prior live-stream study: debugging is 41 percent editing and 29 percent testing. Cites one study of automated debugging tools: modest benefit for novices, not general.
limits: Related-work claims, quoted second-hand. The grounding of textbook advice is unclear, as the authors note.
agent_relevance: Do not instruct the agent to read the whole system first. Target reading by hypothesis.

source: Alaboudi and LaToza (2020) Using Hypotheses as a Debugging Aid
finding: Developers hold few hypotheses and most early ones are wrong. A correct hypothesis early strongly predicts success.
numbers: 20 developers in control: median 1 hypothesis in stage 1 (27 total, 3 correct = 11 percent); stage 2: 35 total, 9 correct (25 percent); stage 3: 38 total, 15 correct (39 percent). A correct hypothesis at stage 2 gave 5 times higher odds of fixing, p = 0.01. 60 sessions across 3 conditions.
limits: Lab tasks (3 tasks, success 90 percent on task 3 vs 55 percent on tasks 1 and 2). Small groups of about 6 to 8 per cell.
agent_relevance: Early wrong hypotheses are the norm. The agent should generate several rival hypotheses at once and score them against evidence.

source: Alaboudi and LaToza (2020) Using Hypotheses as a Debugging Aid
finding: Intervention test. Handing developers fault locations did not help. Handing them candidate hypotheses did.
numbers: Fault locations: no gain in correct hypotheses (stage 2 p = 0.41, stage 3 p = 0.13) and no gain in fixing (p = 0.67). Candidate hypotheses: about 6 times more likely to fix (p = 0.039); a stronger predictor than years of experience.
limits: Small N; the odds ratio has a wide interval. The offered hypotheses were written by the authors.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that why it might be broken is better help than where to look. Supply the agent with candidate causes, not only file lists.

source: Alaboudi and LaToza (2021) An Exploratory Study of Debugging Episodes
finding: Debugging takes a large and very uneven share of programming sessions. A few long episodes hold most of the time.
numbers: Debugging episodes were 13 to 95 percent of session time, mean 48 percent, sd 24. Log-based estimates were 14 percent; self-reports 20 to 60 percent. 80 percent of episode time came from 25 episodes. 91 percent of developers consulted external resources; 92 percent of searches were for an API explanation rather than defect behaviour (8 percent).
limits: Re-analysis of recorded sessions, not a controlled test. Sample is mostly open-source developers.
agent_relevance: Long-tail effort: a few hard bugs dominate. Plan stop and escalate rules for the long tail.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: Self-repair gains are modest once compute cost is counted. The bottleneck is the quality of the diagnosis (feedback on why code failed).
numbers: Human feedback (16 participants, 40 failing programs, 2 feedbacks each) vs GPT-4 own feedback: overall repair success 52.60 vs 33.30 percent. Introductory 62.21 vs 42.64, interview 45.67 vs 19.33, competition 14.67 vs 3.67 percent. Stronger-model feedback gave larger gains than own feedback.
limits: Short competitive programs (HumanEval, APPS), not repository debugging. Human study was small and online, about 1 hour each.
agent_relevance: Quality of the explanation of the failure matters more than the number of repair tries. Invest in S2 diagnosis before patching.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: Code Llama, GPT-3.5, GPT-4: self-repair sometimes gives no gain over drawing more samples at equal compute.
numbers: Abstract: gains are often modest, vary a lot between subsets of the data, and are sometimes not present at all.
quote: gains are often modest, vary a lot between subsets of the data, and are sometimes not present at all
limits: Boundary condition: depends on compute-matched baseline and on model strength.
agent_relevance: Always compare against a resample baseline when judging a repair loop.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) debug-gym: A Text-Based Environment for Interactive Debugging
finding: Giving an LLM agent a Python debugger (pdb) to gather runtime evidence helps strong models on repo-level bugs but can hurt weak ones.
numbers: SWE-bench-Lite, 3 runs: Claude 3.7 Sonnet rewrite 37.2, debug 48.4, debug(5) 52.1 percent (column mapping from garbled table text). Text states weaker models (GPT-4o, 4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B) did worse with pdb from the start; debug(5) beat rewrite for all models.
limits: Table text was garbled in extraction; only the Claude 3.7 row is confidently read. Minimal prompts, 20-step history. Authors say agents are far from using tools well. On simple Aider tasks pdb gave no clear effect.
agent_relevance: Debugger evidence helps only if the model can use it. Offer tools after a few failed rewrites (debug(5) pattern) rather than from step 1.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) debug-gym
finding: Qualitative: on Mini-nightmare (10 hand-built bugs) only reasoning-strong backbones inferred the cause from failing tests; weaker ones kept rewriting the wrong code.
numbers: GPT-4o and Llama-3.3-70B kept rewriting input-parsing code; R1-Distill-70B and Claude 3.7 Sonnet identified the line-number range problem; Claude solved it with one rewrite after breakpoint and print commands.
limits: Ten tasks, three runs, anecdotal trajectories.
agent_relevance: Failure to form a cause hypothesis shows up as repeated patching of the same region. Detect and break that loop.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents
finding: A fixed three-phase pipeline (localize, repair, validate) with no autonomous tool decisions matched or beat open-source agents on SWE-bench Lite at low cost. Rival view: do agents need a free-form evolving model at all?
numbers: 32.00 percent (96 of 300) resolved, 0.70 dollars per issue with GPT-4o. Authors found problem items with leaked patches or misleading issues and built Lite-S.
limits: Benchmark is SWE-bench Lite; later agents surpassed it. Hierarchical localisation is itself a built-in model of the repo.
agent_relevance: A staged, structured evidence gather can beat free exploration. S2 may need structure (file, class, line) more than freedom.

source: Aleithan et al. (2024) SWE-Bench+: Enhanced Coding Benchmark for LLMs
finding: Large part of agent success on SWE-bench is not real debugging: answers leak into the issue text and tests are weak.
numbers: 32.67 percent of SWE-Agent+GPT-4 successes had solution leakage; 31.08 percent passed on weak tests. After filtering, resolution fell from 12.47 to 3.97 percent. 94 percent of instances predate model cutoffs.
limits: One agent and model studied; manual screening.
agent_relevance: Measure our agent on leak-free sets. Do not count issue-text answers as evidence of building a model.

source: Majgaonkar et al. (2025) Understanding Code Agent Behaviour
finding: Agents usually reach the right file even when they fail. Failure is more about the edit than about navigation.
numbers: Correct problematic files identified in 72 to 81 percent of trajectories even in failures (SWE-Bench Lite). Failed trajectories longer: SWE-agent 12.6 percent (Lite) and 18.5 percent (Verified) longer; OpenHands 31.0 and 82.5 percent longer. Per a search-result summary (not checked in text), 35 to 40 percent of failures on Verified miss correct files entirely.
limits: Three agents only. The length-failure link is later shown to be confounded (next lines).
agent_relevance: Locating is easier than understanding. Spend effort on testing the model of why the code is wrong.

source: Mehtiyev and Assuncao (2026) Beyond Resolution Rates
finding: Failed replication of a popular claim. The link 'longer trajectory means failure' reverses when task difficulty is controlled.
numbers: 9,374 trajectories, 19 agents, 14 LLMs, 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks. Within 416 contested tasks, resolved runs averaged 44.0 steps vs 39.6 for failed; resolved longer on 263 of 416 tasks (63 percent), p = 1.9e-9 (Wilcoxon).
limits: Verified set only; correlation, not intervention.
agent_relevance: Do not use step count alone as a stuck signal. Use lack of new evidence instead.

source: Mehtiyev and Assuncao (2026) Beyond Resolution Rates
finding: Gathering context before editing and investing in validation separates successes from failures. These habits come from the agent framework, not adapted to the task.
numbers: Authors report this holds after controlling for difficulty. 12 never-solved tasks needed only simple patches but all agents failed because of gaps in architectural reasoning and domain knowledge.
limits: Strategy is agent-determined, so effect may reflect which framework is strong. No random assignment of strategy.
agent_relevance: Add a rule: no edit before an explicit evidence-gathering step. The weak spot is architectural understanding, which fits the S2 model.

source: Mehtiyev and Assuncao (2026) Beyond Resolution Rates
finding: The base model matters more than the scaffold, and the scaffold gap shrinks with stronger models.
numbers: Switching LLM moves resolution by 51.5 pp across 6 LLMs in SWE-agent and 31.5 pp across 6 in OpenHands. Framework gap with LLM fixed: 19.4 pp, 3.8 pp, 0.9 pp over three model generations; at the frontier 5 frameworks are within 10 pp of the best.
limits: Competing explanation for scaffold benefit. Applies to coding agent frameworks, not general thinking schemas.
agent_relevance: Expect scaffold gains for evidence gathering to be larger on weaker models. Test on our target model.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Coherence Collapse (TrajEval)
finding: Capable models often reach and edit the correct function, then fail anyway. The weak point is keeping a coherent model across edits.
numbers: 16,758 trajectories, 3 architectures, 7 models. 60 to 69 percent of failures on SWE-Agent and OpenHands (GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, Qwen3-Coder, Qwen3-235B) edit the right functions but give a wrong patch. In 5 cases the agent produced the gold patch mid-run and destroyed it later; an edit-commit checkpoint recovered all 5. Consensus variant gave +3.0 pp Pass@1 (p = 0.08).
limits: Reference-patch-aligned analysis; the +3.0 pp is not significant at 0.05. Contrasts with the older finding that localisation is the main failure.
agent_relevance: Keep a committed best-known state and test before overwrite. A running model must resist thrash.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reasoning Runtime Behavior of a Program with LLM: How Far Are We? (REval)
finding: LLMs poorly predict intermediate execution behaviour and are inconsistent across steps, even when the final output is right.
numbers: Average accuracy 44.4 percent on runtime behavior reasoning; Incremental Consistency score 10.3 on average. Chain of thought raised execution path prediction from 10.8 to 21.4 percent for a small model.
limits: Older open code models mostly; 2025 reasoning models score higher (next line).
agent_relevance: Do not trust the model to simulate execution in its head. Run the code.

source: Abdollahi et al. (2025) Demystifying Errors in LLM Reasoning Traces: Code Execution Simulation
finding: Newer reasoning models simulate execution well but still make nine kinds of errors. A calculator-style tool fixes part.
numbers: 427 snippets, 12 inputs each (regular, edge, invalid). DeepSeek-R1, o4-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude 4 Sonnet: 85 to 98 percent accuracy. Tool augmentation corrected 58 percent of the computation-error category.
limits: Short, self-contained snippets from HumanEval+ and LiveCodeBench, not systems.
agent_relevance: Mental simulation is reliable on small units; delegate arithmetic and long state tracking to tools.

source: Gu et al. (2024) CRUXEval
finding: Output and input prediction for short functions is far from solved, and it is not predicted by HumanEval ranking.
numbers: GPT-4 pass@1 67 percent (input) and 63 percent (output); with chain of thought 75 and 81 percent. Best open models 47 and 44 percent; Code Llama 34B 50 and 46 percent with CoT.
limits: 2024 models; saturating as reasoning models arrived.
agent_relevance: Chain of thought helps mental execution of small functions.

source: Gugerty and Olson (1986) Debugging by skilled and novice programmers
finding: Classic founding comparison of skilled and novice debuggers. Not opened this session; listed so the gap is visible.
numbers: Not recorded: full text not read.
limits: Only metadata seen via OpenAlex (75 citations). Do not cite numbers.
agent_relevance: Check the numbers before any use; the opened modern studies above carry the evidence.

source: Parnin and Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers?
finding: Frequently cited study where automated fault ranking did not clearly help real programmers. Not opened this session.
numbers: Not recorded: full text not read (587 citations in OpenAlex).
limits: Second-hand: Li and Coblenz say one study found modest benefit for novices but not general improvement.
agent_relevance: Consistent with the Alaboudi null result for fault locations.

source: Beller et al. (2018) On the dichotomy of debugging behavior among programmers
finding: Reports that many developers avoid the IDE debugger and rely on print statements. Not opened (PDF fetch failed).
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Metadata only (78 citations).
agent_relevance: Li and Coblenz cite a similar claim: only a minority use IDE debugging tools.

source: Majgaonkar et al. (2025) vs Kim et al. (2026): rival accounts of agent failure
finding: Competing explanations: wrong place (35 to 40 percent of Verified failures miss correct files, secondhand) vs wrong edit (60 to 69 percent of capable-model failures reach correct functions). Which dominates depends on model strength and agent.
numbers: See the Majgaonkar and Kim lines above.
limits: Different failure definitions (file-level vs function-level), agents and models.
agent_relevance: The schema must cover both localisation and edit coherence, with weights by model strength.
